Medical History

- Current health issues and chronic disease risk factors (e.g., hypertension, diabetes):  3 days of watery, non-bloody diarrhea (~6–7/day) with intermittent crampy left lower abdominal pain; initial vomiting now resolved; subjective fever/hot feeling at onset; loss of appetite; feeling weak/shaky; tolerating fluids. Past history of asthma (reported well-controlled). Possible foodborne trigger after Chinese restaurant meal ~4 days ago.
- Family history of chronic conditions (e.g., CVD, diabetes):  Not recorded.
- Current medications including OTC and traditional medicines:  Asthma inhaler—dose/route/frequency not documented. No other regular medications reported. Paracetamol/acetaminophen advised “two tablets up to four times daily” for fever/aches—strength not documented. Oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte) recommended.

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Summary: Acute onset of watery, non-bloody diarrhea with intermittent crampy LLQ pain for 3 days, initial vomiting now resolved, subjective fever at onset, maintaining hydration, likely triggered by recent restaurant meal; household contact with vomiting only. Past history of well-controlled asthma; no red flags (no blood in stool, no persistent vomiting).
- Differentials (consistent with DDx):
  - Acute viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus): Supported by short, self-limiting course, vomiting at onset, subjective fever, and household contact with vomiting.
  - Acute bacterial gastroenteritis/foodborne infection (e.g., Salmonella, ETEC, Campylobacter): Temporal association with restaurant meal and fever/crampy pain.
  - Less likely: Toxin-mediated food poisoning (longer onset and course than typical), diverticulitis (pain intermittent and diarrhea predominant).
- Working diagnosis: Acute gastroenteritis, likely viral.
- Plan:
  - Conservative management: Maintain hydration; use oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte).
  - Symptom control: Paracetamol/acetaminophen up to two tablets four times daily for fever/aches (strength not documented).
  - Rest: Advise 2–3 days off work.
  - Monitoring/follow-up: If no improvement in 3–4 days, return for reassessment; consider stool testing if persistent symptoms.
  - No antibiotics indicated at this time per clinician discussion.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Acute viral gastroenteritis (High): Short course of watery, non-bloody diarrhea with initial vomiting and subjective fever; household contact with vomiting supports viral etiology.
- Acute bacterial gastroenteritis/foodborne infection (Medium): Onset ~1 day after restaurant meal with fever/crampy pain is compatible despite absence of blood.
- Diverticulitis (Low): LLQ pain noted, but intermittent cramps with predominant diarrhea and no focal peritoneal signs make this less likely.
